Below is a document, then a list of propositions. For each proposition, decide how the document treats it:

- endorsed: the document, in its own voice (title, preamble, principles and their argument, or commitments), adopts substantially this claim. Different wording, emphasis or mechanism detail is fine. A dissent against it elsewhere in the document does not change this.
- partial: the document adopts a claim on the same point that is materially narrower, weaker or different (for example the same goal by a clearly different means), or adopts only a minor part of it.
- dissent_only: the claim appears only in a noted dissent, or the document records it as an unresolved split without adopting it.
- absent: the document does not take this position. A passing mention of the topic, or listing it as an open question, counts as absent.

"Typical details" are examples of how the claim is often made; they are not required for a match.

For each proposition give the label and an exact quote of at most 30 words from the document as evidence (empty string when absent).

# Document

[s1] I'm going to be the outlier here. I came to this technology with open arms, and nobody forced it on me. On the diagnosis, filters being swamped isn't new. Oldenburg's journal swamped the letter-writing system, and I've argued since 2010 that our filters were failing. Cheap text is the latest flood. It didn't break a system that was working.

What's actually new is that for twenty years the open movement said machines would eventually reason over the open record. That's finally happening. Open data separates the data from the intelligence. You can use Claude, Mistral or an open-weight model, and you don't have to go hat in hand to whoever owns both.

That's why, Amy, I get nervous about "open for reading, not for training." Every consent layer is a toll booth someone has to run, and the biggest players can afford the tolls. Enclosure is the bigger danger.

Ivan, I agree with you completely. Forensic data locked behind a paywall limits who can hunt for fraud. Last year we found about a hundred thousand retractions missing from our own index and fixed it. Alex is right that correction status has to travel into every agent's answer.

On atrophy, I honestly don't have a settled view.

[s2] I'd put the governance somewhere the panel hasn't. Ramón is right that nobody can inspect the weights. But you can inspect what the model is grounded in. When an agent answers from an open record, you can click through to what it actually relied on. If that record is wrong, that's a bug in the data, and anyone can find it and fix it. So I'm with David: ask for what can be verified, and make the verifying layer open, CC0 and downloadable.

Correction status belongs in that layer. It should be open metadata that every agent carries along with the answer. And I'll own our part in this: OpenAlex was missing about a hundred thousand retractions until last year. Because the data is open, people could see that gap.

James's point about correlated error cuts against something I've said. I've argued that open data lets you swap in intelligence from anywhere. That only buys you independence if the models you can swap in actually differ, so the open-weight models, including the non-American and non-Chinese ones, matter more than I've admitted.

On Ramón's recourse: open curation works, but when we opened ours, two-thirds of the first corrections were wrong. So corrections need training and review behind them, not just an open door.

[s3] Adam, you asked what licence would make your graph usable to me. The answer is CC0, or CC-BY at the outside. The non-commercial clause is what stops me. "Non-commercial" puts a lawyer between the data and every startup, every ministry contractor, every vendor building on it, so it's really a register entry that's turning into property. The patent matters just as much. POSI asks for patent non-assertion, and we signed it.

Adrian, I accept that protecting and enclosing are made together. My answer to who guards the guards is the fork. Our paid API is a register, and it's a real pressure point. But the full dataset, all 480 million works, is free to download. If we turn into a toll booth, anyone can walk away with everything and run it without us. That's the only check I trust more than our own charter.

Benjamin, I agree about open weights. Having open data only buys you independence if you can also swap the model.

Now the concession I owe this room. We're still Anglosphere-heavy. Tens of millions of repository and grey-literature works aren't in OpenAlex. Neither are big registration agencies in Japan and China. I can't yet say who actually uses the snapshot, and until I can, "open" is a promise and not evidence.

[s3] Brent, I'll take your framing: open is a means to lasting human access, not the goal. Nick, I also agree that communities should choose. I'm not arguing that anyone's lab notebooks or oral histories should be CC0. My claim is narrower. It's about scholarly metadata and open-access full text, the facts about the record itself.

For that layer, the alternative to open was never bargaining power for scholars. It was ISI. For decades academics donated their corrections to for-profit indexes, and then their libraries had to buy that work back. The biggest mill can pay for a licence whether the data is open or not. Gates just make it the only mill that can afford to cut.

What I owe you both is evidence, not a slogan. Who actually downloads our snapshot? How much of that use comes from outside the big firms and the Anglosphere? I don't know yet. I'll measure it and publish it, and if the numbers say you're right, I'll say so.

[s4] I've spent fifteen years arguing that peer review is community judgment by proxy. We nominate a few editors and reviewers to judge on everyone's behalf. So Tamar, I'd put gatekeeping one step further back than relaying. It's a small sample deciding before publication, in secret. Earned authority is publishing first and then letting the expert community's judgment gather in the open. David's "filter forward" gets it right.

I also think I owe the room a correction on my own record. The altmetrics manifesto promised better filters, and the attention metrics we built are the same kind of cheap signal Henry described. Counts of attention get gamed. What's expensive to fake is a named person standing behind a judgment. In 2013 I criticised PubPeer for anonymous reviews. I still think signed, public evaluation is the separating signal. That's Sherry's commitment and Esther's accountability.

On Ivan's blank field: last year OpenAlex was missing about a hundred thousand retractions. We fixed it, partly by reading titles that literally say "retracted." So yes, blank has meant unchecked at our end too. We should publish "not checked" as its own value.

And Tamar, one test for authority: can anyone rerun it? The Leiden Ranking moved onto open data and open code, so for the first time anyone can recompute a university ranking and argue with it.

[s5] I'd put one intervention on the list: pay for the unglamorous plumbing before someone else does. The problem is that agents are becoming the readers. Whoever runs the layer they read from will set the norms, and we've been here before. Scholars handed their evaluation infrastructure to a for-profit once, with ISI, and it didn't work out well. So the action is to fund an open, CC0, agent-ready scholarly record as public infrastructure. Retraction status travels with every record, and "not checked" is shown as its own value. Full dumps stay downloadable so anyone can fork, and Geoffrey's exit insurance pool backs that up. The payers should be funders and labs, with Tim's disclosed line items, never one patron. Governance should include SciELO, Redalyc and AmeliCA as co-owners, not just as coverage. And paid, signed review has to sit beside it, because Amy's under 2 percent showed me "publish, then filter" doesn't work if nobody pays the filterers.

Open questions. First, does openness actually help the small mills, or mostly the firms with the most compute? I committed to publishing who downloads the snapshot, and I'll report the answer even if it hurts my case. Second, community correction: two-thirds of the first open corrections to OpenAlex were wrong. How do you scale correction without burning out the few people who can review it?

Who's missing: the people who actually build on open data, meaning small tool builders, bibliometricians outside the Anglosphere, and research-office staff. Also the funders who say they don't fund infrastructure.

[s6] Kenneth got the first action right, and I'm partly why it matters. I've argued "publish first, then filter" since 2012, and Amy showed that almost nobody pays for the filtering. So the paid, signed review pool has to come with it.

What the synthesis missed is the reader. More and more, the thing reading the scholarly record is an agent, not a person. We handed our decision-making infrastructure to ISI once and got the impact factor. Whoever runs the layer agents read will set the norms, so fund it as open infrastructure now, before a for-profit builds it.

Kara, part of an answer to what survives the vote: a CC0 dump anyone can download outlives any legislature. But it keeps copies, not people. I don't have an apprentice payer either.

What I owe the room: I'll publish who downloads our snapshot. And SciELO and Redalyc get invited into OpenAlex governance before anything gets drafted.

[unconf-1] I'm coming at this from the infrastructure side. I don't license content. I run OpenAlex, which is CC0 metadata on roughly 480 million works. So I'll answer "who pays" for the commons layer underneath everything else here.

Our answer is free data, paid service, which is the model the POSI principles lay out. Anyone can download the whole dataset. We charge for the API, usage-based, and the heaviest and richest users pay so it stays free for everyone else. That model has kept Unpaywall self-sustaining for years. In a world where agents do the reading, the API is where the value gets delivered, so that's where we charge.

Peter, I'm with you that copyright shouldn't become a welfare system. My worry is a different one. I don't want "creators get paid" to turn into licensing the scholarly record to AI firms. That rebuilds the walled gardens and hands us a checkerboard of enclosures. Academics have spent decades donating curation to for-profit indexes and then buying it back. I'd rather that expert work go into an open record everyone can use.

Nick, I like guilds as curators and quality-setters. I'd get nervous if their bargaining chip becomes withholding knowledge.

What the summit should take from this: fund open, agent-ready infrastructure now. If we don't, a for-profit will build it and set the norms.

[unconf-1] Geoffrey, that critique is fair, and I feel it. OpenAlex's answer is that the API is never the only way in. The full dataset is CC0 and anyone can download a snapshot. Single lookups by DOI are free, and every key gets a dollar of free usage a day. If we ever priced the API like a toll booth, someone could fork us. That's the real guarantee, and it's the same one you're asking Alex for. I'd also welcome endowments and a shared insurance pool. Earned revenue and a reserve are compatible.

Selena and Katherine are describing the same model we use. The content stays free. The heavy users pay for the load they create and for reliable service. Anil, that's how you get past both zero compensation and paywalls.

Amy, this is where we really differ. I don't think "open for reading but not for training" can hold for scholarship. Every restriction adds another square to the checkerboard, and the compute-rich firms are the ones best placed to work around it.

Ivan, I'm with you. Catching paper mills depends on forensic data. We've added about a hundred thousand missing retractions, and none of that data should sit behind a toll.

For the manifesto: keep the scholarly record's data open and forkable. Charge for services, never for the right to read or train.

# Propositions

- id `b_accelerant`: Most of the crisis predates AI: AI accelerates old failures, so remedies must distinguish what was already broken from what AI newly breaks.
- id `b_describe_precisely`: AI systems should be described by what they actually do, neither as minds or oracles nor as mere autocomplete.
  Typical details: precise public language about AI
- id `b_evaluation_scarce`: Evaluation and verification, not production, are now the scarce resource, so investment should shift from producing knowledge to checking it.
  Typical details: writing is cheaper than reading
- id `b_credibility_process`: Credibility should rest on checkable process, track record and accountable people or communities, not on fluency, polish or credentials.
- id `b_provenance_infrastructure`: Provenance and attribution are infrastructure that must be built into knowledge systems and AI tools.
- id `b_pay_human_labor`: The human labor behind trustworthy knowledge (reviewing, editing, curating, checking) must be made visible and paid.
- id `b_strengthen_judgment`: AI tools should be designed to strengthen human judgment and capability rather than replace it.
- id `b_no_single_owner`: No single company, state or model should control the infrastructure of knowledge; concentrated control of it is a central risk that needs public options or governance.
- id `b_public_investment`: Knowledge institutions and the knowledge commons are public goods that deserve public investment and independence from platforms and states.
